Web and Application Services

1. Web and Application Services

HarborStatus now has a purpose: a client on the isolated lab network should receive the current status page from the intended server. Installing a package is only one step. A request crosses name resolution, network policy, a listening socket, a virtual host, filesystem access, and application behavior. This chapter turns those layers into a service you can test.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — Chapter 19 — Web and Application Services

2. Verify the actual web-service contract

A listener is not the same as trusted TLS or the approved release marker. Test each required property. A successful HTTP status hides the wrong deployed content.

SOURCE: Verify the actual web-service contract

3. Chapter 19 — Web and Application Services

HarborStatus now has a purpose: a client on the isolated lab network should receive the current status page from the intended server. Installing a package is only one step. A request crosses name resolution, network policy, a listening socket, a virtual host, filesystem access, and application behavior. This chapter turns those layers into a service you can test.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — Chapter 19 — Web and Application Services

4. 19.1 Server Daemons

A daemon is a process that provides a background service. Modern daemons commonly remain in the foreground while systemd supervises them. “Background service” describes the operating role; it does not require the program to detach itself or end its command with &.

Separate installation, configuration, process supervision, and user-visible health. A package can be installed without a running process. A process can run without listening on the expected address. A listener can accept connections while returning the wrong website. Record one test for each claim instead of allowing a green service status to stand for all four.

Use the package’s service unit unless you have a specific reason to replace it. Vendor units can include environment setup, shutdown behavior, and security controls that a homemade unit omits. Review local differences through systemctl cat nginx before changing them.

Linux example — 19.1

Inspect the web daemon and its process identity.

What to check: Some master processes spawn workers under another identity; inspect the actual worker.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.1 Server Daemons

6. 19.2 Ports and Sockets

An Internet socket combines an address, transport protocol, and port. A service listening on 127.0.0.1:8080 accepts local IPv4 connections, not connections arriving at the server’s network address. 0.0.0.0:8080 means all local IPv4 addresses, which can expose more interfaces than intended. IPv6 listening and dual-stack behavior must be checked separately.

The first command inspects TCP listeners and, with sufficient permission, their processes. The second sends an HTTP request. Neither establishes that a remote client is allowed through a firewall. Unix-domain sockets use a filesystem-associated address rather than an IP port; their access depends on path permissions and service configuration.

Linux example — 19.2

List listening network and Unix sockets.

What to check: A Unix socket is not an IP listening port; permissions and namespaces still matter.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.2 Ports and Sockets

9. 19.3 Apache HTTP Server

Apache organizes behavior through modules and configuration directives. In the RHEL family, the common package and unit name is httpd; on Ubuntu and Debian it is apache2. Their configuration directory layouts and module-enabling conventions differ. Do not copy a Debian path into a RHEL playbook and assume installation translates everything else.

Use the distribution’s configuration-test wrapper before reload: commonly apachectl configtest on RHEL-family installations and apache2ctl configtest on Ubuntu. Inspect virtual-host selection with the corresponding -S invocation. A syntax test checks configuration, not certificate trust, content correctness, or external reachability. Name-based virtual hosts allow several sites to share an address while retaining separate configuration. (R43)

Choose Apache or NGINX for this lab rather than installing both and competing for port 80. Either can serve a simple static site. Operational familiarity, required modules, and application integration matter more than declaring a universal winner.

Linux example — 19.3

Validate Apache using the installed distribution's command.

What to check: Use the branch for your installation and investigate warnings before reload.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.3 Apache HTTP Server

11. 19.4 NGINX

NGINX reads a hierarchical configuration with contexts such as http, server, and location. Distribution packages normally arrange a top-level file that includes smaller files. Establish those include paths on your actual host. An example placed in an unreferenced directory has no effect.

Run the reload only after the test succeeds and after confirming the unit is already running. Reloading asks the existing service to apply configuration; starting a stopped service is a different action. NGINX’s master and workers coordinate configuration changes and ongoing requests. The application’s observable outcome still needs verification after reload. (R44)

nginx -T prints the complete configuration as well as testing it. That is useful for tracing includes, but its output may contain sensitive settings. Keep it in an appropriately protected incident record, not a public paste.

Linux example — 19.4

Validate NGINX configuration without reloading it.

What to check: A successful syntax and file-access check does not verify the served page.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.4 NGINX

14. 19.5 Virtual Hosts

A virtual host maps a request to site-specific settings. For HTTP, the destination address and port select a listener, and the requested host name helps select a site. For HTTPS, the TLS handshake can select a certificate using Server Name Indication before the HTTP request is processed.

A successful request to the IP address can therefore return a default site while the named site is broken. Preserve the name while overriding DNS for a controlled test:

Replace the address with the verified lab server. This tests that address with the intended HTTP host name, but deliberately does not test normal DNS resolution. Run a second request without --resolve when DNS is part of the acceptance test.

Linux example — 19.5

Test host-based selection on the Chapter 19 lab server.

What to check: The lab address and hostname must match your topology; check the intended release marker.

NGINX virtual-host candidate

Place this candidate only in an included http-context location on the isolated chapter lab. Check duplicate server definitions, permissions, labels, nginx -t, and the hostname-specific client response.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.5 Virtual Hosts

18. 19.6 TLS Certificates

TLS encrypts a connection and, when the client correctly verifies the certificate, authenticates the named endpoint. A certificate connects a public key to identities under an issuer’s policy. The corresponding private key must remain protected. Merely enabling encryption does not establish trustworthy server identity.

Check the requested name against the certificate’s Subject Alternative Name, its validity interval, the chain supplied by the server, and the client’s trust store. A .test lab name needs a deliberate private trust arrangement; it is not a candidate for an ordinary publicly trusted certificate. Chapter 33 uses an explicitly trusted, short-lived lab certificate and separates that exercise from production issuance.

Do not turn curl -k into a monitoring solution. It disables a control you should be testing. Distribute an approved CA certificate or supply an explicit trust file for a bounded lab test. Renewal also needs a deployment and reload path, not just creation of a new certificate file. (R45)

Linux example — 19.6

Inspect the capstone public certificate.

What to check: Requires the RHEL capstone certificate; the hostname should appear in SAN and dates must cover current time.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.6 TLS Certificates

20. 19.7 Reverse Proxies

A reverse proxy receives a client request and forwards it to an application. This can concentrate TLS handling and public listeners while leaving an application bound to a private address. It also introduces another failure boundary: the proxy can be healthy while its upstream is unavailable.

An illustrative NGINX location for a separately installed application is:

This example deliberately replaces, rather than trusts, a client-supplied forwarding chain at a single edge proxy. The application must trust such headers only from that proxy. The lack of a URI after the upstream address preserves the request URI here. Adding a trailing slash changes URI replacement behavior. Understand that difference before applying a configuration to an application’s route structure. Proxy read timeouts apply between read operations, not necessarily as a total transaction deadline. (R44)

Linux example — 19.7

Probe a configured lab reverse proxy.

What to check: A 502 can indicate an upstream failure; inspect the proxy error log and backend separately.

NGINX reverse-proxy candidate

This loopback-only lab candidate assumes a reviewed backend on port 9000. The backend must trust forwarded headers only from the approved proxy; validate the complete NGINX configuration before reload.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.7 Reverse Proxies

24. 19.8 Application Services

An application needs an executable, dependencies, configuration, a runtime identity, a working directory, and a supervised lifecycle. Declare writable state separately from read-only release files. A Python virtual environment or a container image packages dependencies; neither supplies a backup strategy or an operational owner.

Distinguish liveness from readiness. Liveness asks whether a process should remain running. Readiness asks whether it can handle its intended traffic. A readiness check may include a critical dependency, but a dependency outage should not automatically cause every application instance to restart continuously.

For HarborStatus, serving a known page with the expected release marker is more informative than checking only that port 80 opens. Later, a dynamic service might require a bounded test transaction with cleanup. Keep health checks cheap, non-destructive, and explicit about the behavior they prove.

Linux example — 19.8

Inspect a service's command and runtime state.

What to check: The managed command can differ from an interactive shell invocation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.8 Application Services

26. 19.9 Service Accounts

A worker serving static files needs to read those files, not edit them. Let a controlled deployment identity or root own release content, with the service receiving read and directory-traversal access. Give writable application state a separate directory with narrower ownership.

Do not change the packaged NGINX worker identity merely to match a tutorial. Common identities include nginx and www-data, but inspect the active configuration. Check every parent directory, not just the page. A readable file under a non-traversable parent is inaccessible to the worker.

Secret material should not share a directory exported as web content. A web configuration error should not transform an application’s backup, private key, or environment file into a downloadable object.

Linux example — 19.9

Resolve the host's web account.

What to check: Inspect the actual process identity rather than relying solely on a distribution convention.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.9 Service Accounts

28. 19.10 Firewall Configuration

Before opening a port, establish which interfaces and source networks need it. Confirm console recovery and retain administrative access. On a firewalld host, inspect active zones and both runtime and permanent settings. On a different host, identify its actual firewall manager instead of adding another one.

Test from an approved remote client and, where authorized, from a source that should be denied. Local requests cannot establish the external rule’s behavior. A cloud network policy can block a connection that the host firewall permits, and a public interface can expose a service that seemed private in a one-interface lab.

Do not open an application backend port when only its reverse proxy should be reachable. The restriction should be true in the binding address, network policy, and documented architecture where practical.

Linux example — 19.10

Inspect active firewalld zones without changing policy.

What to check: Requires firewalld; test the intended client source separately from localhost.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.10 Firewall Configuration

30. 19.11 SELinux Considerations

On the enforcing RHEL-family VM, apply Chapter 18’s persistent mapping for /srv/harbor/site. Use httpd_sys_content_t for read-only web content, not a broadly writable type. Check parent traversal, worker domain, and recent AVC events when a request fails.

An approved reverse proxy may require an SELinux policy interface allowing outbound connections. Inspect available booleans and the denied operation before choosing one. Enabling a broad networking boolean is a policy decision, not an automatic part of installing NGINX. A static site does not need outbound application access merely because a reverse-proxy tutorial does. (R39)

Linux example — 19.11

Inspect labels and recent web-service denials on SELinux.

What to check: Keep policy enforcing and diagnose the exact attempted operation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.11 SELinux Considerations

32. 19.12 Troubleshooting Web Services

Trace one failing request through layers. First identify the exact URL, client location, time, and symptom. Then verify name resolution, route, listener, TLS, virtual host, content access, and upstream behavior as applicable. Record what each test bypasses.

A 403 response indicates the server processed a request and refused access under some rule; it does not uniquely identify Unix permissions. A 404 can arise from the wrong virtual host or routing rule rather than a missing release file. A 502 or 504 often directs attention toward the upstream path, but use the proxy’s error log to determine the actual failure.

Collect systemctl status, a bounded journal window, application errors, and a response body or header sample with secrets removed. Resist restarting several layers simultaneously: that destroys the comparison needed to identify the cause.

Linux example — 19.12

Combine configuration, listener, and request tests.

What to check: A default-site response is not proof that the intended virtual host is correct.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — 19.12 Troubleshooting Web Services

34. Requirement and preconditions

On a disposable VM, NGINX must serve a root-owned page from /srv/harbor/site to the approved lab client. Port 80 is unused. Existing NGINX configuration, if any, is backed up and understood. The site has no confidential content. This first exercise uses isolated-network HTTP; production TLS is addressed in the capstone.

Install from the distribution’s supported repository. Choose one branch:

Inspect whether installation started the service. Package installation can have side effects, so the VM must already be isolated and its firewall understood.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — Requirement and preconditions

35. Requirement and preconditions · example 1

On a disposable VM, NGINX must serve a root-owned page from /srv/harbor/site to the approved lab client. Port 80 is unused. Existing NGINX configuration, if any, is backed up and understood. The site has no confidential content. This first exercise uses isolated-network HTTP; production TLS is addressed in the capstone.

Install from the distribution’s supported repository. Choose one branch:

Inspect whether installation started the service. Package installation can have side effects, so the VM must already be isolated and its firewall understood.

37. Create content and configuration

Apply Chapter 18’s mapping on the SELinux VM. Verify that /etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf is included inside the http context. Create /etc/nginx/conf.d/harbor-status.conf with sudoedit:

This is a server block, not a replacement for the entire nginx.conf. Do not overwrite unknown production configuration. Existing default sites can remain for this named-site test as long as there is no conflicting server-name definition.

Stop at a failed validation. A start or reload following a failure does not make the file correct. The response should contain the exact release marker; that is an expected observation, not a claimed execution result on your VM.

41. Verify the complete path and rollback

Apply only the approved lab firewall exception, then request the site from the client with --resolve. Confirm a corresponding access-log record and check for recent SELinux denials. Finally test ordinary resolution once the lab resolver or client hosts file is deliberately configured.

For rollback, restore the prior configuration and content, run the syntax test, reload, and repeat the original request. Remove only rules and label mappings introduced by this exercise when retiring it. A rollback that restores files but not the served page has not restored the service.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — Verify the complete path and rollback

42. Verify the complete path and rollback · example 1

Apply only the approved lab firewall exception, then request the site from the client with --resolve. Confirm a corresponding access-log record and check for recent SELinux denials. Finally test ordinary resolution once the lab resolver or client hosts file is deliberately configured.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — Verify the complete path and rollback

43. Practice and implementation lab

Create a second named site with a different harmless marker. Demonstrate why requesting only the IP address is not a reliable test of either name. Intentionally misspell the lab site’s document root, capture the error, restore the correct root, and explain which layers continued to work during the fault.

Check your understanding. Can active (running) prove that clients receive the right site? No. Does a trusted TLS connection prove the application’s answer is correct? No. Should a static web worker own its release files? Ordinarily no; read access is sufficient.

Chapter takeaway. A web service is a verified request path, not merely an installed package or running daemon.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch021.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

44. Verify a release marker rather than any page

Read a local response fixture. Real release acceptance also checks endpoint, status and trusted TLS. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Verify a release marker rather than any page
